cards.headline: Trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi conclude without breakthrough

pages.text: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States aimed at ending the nearly five-year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion have concluded after a second day without a meaningful breakthrough. While U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff stated they saw “some openings” and “opportunities,” no agreement was reached to end the conflict. The meetings focused on the “security architecture” of Europe, a framework involving how nations ensure regional stability and defense. For Kyiv, this includes seeking reassurances of allied aid if attacked again despite not being a NATO member. For Moscow, a reworked framework would likely include limiting NATO's influence in eastern Europe, a central Kremlin concern regarding the alliance's eastward expansion.

Despite the lack of a peace settlement, Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange is in the works and could be carried out soon. Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky noted the agreement was “in principle,” while Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff's information department, told Russian state TV it could be one of the biggest swaps after 1,000 soldiers returned home. The exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team described this round—the first since February—as “one of the hardest,” suggesting Russians arrived with “very strict directives.” Conversely, Medinsky stated that much depends on Ukraine, the position of the U.S., and whether Europe “comes to its senses.”

Following the Abu Dhabi sessions, it was announced that on November 5, 2026, U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, will travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and then to Dublin, Ireland, to speak with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. This follows comments from Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who stated on November 11 that three negotiating clusters have been opened. Hours after the second day of negotiations in Abu Dhabi concluded, Russia launched ballistic missiles at Kyiv, Ukraine. Explosions were reported in the capital around 1 a.m. following warnings from Ukraine's Air Force. Attacks against the city are ongoing, and precise targets have not yet been identified.

cards.headline: Suspect faces terrorism charges in Jordan over fatal police stabbing

pages.text: Prosecutors in Amman, Jordan, have charged a suspect with two terrorism-related offenses following a stabbing attack that killed one police officer and injured another. The case has been referred to the State Security Court for trial, according to a November 11, 2026, report from the Jordan News Agency. Brig. Military Judge Ahmed Talat Shahaltough, the State Security Court’s attorney general, stated the suspect was charged under Jordan’s 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law with committing an armed terrorist act resulting in death and carrying out an armed terrorist act. These charges follow a November 5 incident on Madina Munawara Street, where Cpl. Jawad Al-Salayta was stabbed to death while on duty near the Sri Lankan embassy. Capt. Firas Al-Ananzeh sustained facial injuries while attempting to apprehend the attacker, who was arrested after a struggle with a police patrol. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said preliminary investigations indicated the suspect had been planning to target security personnel.

The stabbing occurred nearly two weeks after an October 23 attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the Karak governorate, an incident that killed nine people and wounded dozens. These events have prompted a debate in Jordan regarding counterterrorism legislation. On November 6, Ibrahim Tarawneh, the speaker of the lower house of parliament, said lawmakers would work with the government to review existing laws, address legal loopholes, and strengthen measures to tackle extremism.

cards.headline: US taxpayer group calls for ICC investigation into Trump and Rubio for aiding Gaza genocide

pages.text: The Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), a group comprising US taxpayers and international human rights lawyers, has officially called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate President Donald Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio. At a press conference in The Hague, Netherlands, the group alleged that the two officials are aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza. Taag filed an Article 15 communication—a mechanism that allows individuals or groups to provide information to the ICC Prosecutor regarding alleged crimes—which the group claims provides enough evidence to meet the legal threshold for arrest warrants for both officials. Taag co-founder Seth Donnelly urged the Office of the Prosecutor to act quickly on the submission, stating that previous attempts to use the US federal court system to stop US official participation in the alleged genocide have failed repeatedly.

The submission to the ICC was compiled over nearly a year and includes sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, whistleblower testimony, firsthand eyewitness accounts, video evidence, and documentation of US military, financial, diplomatic, and political support for Israel. Contributors to the evidence include Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon who completed two missions in Gaza, and David McIntosh, a former contractor with the now-defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation. Taag stated that the compiled proof demonstrates that Israel could not have carried out the actions described as genocide by the United Nations and Holocaust scholars without US support. This request follows existing ICC actions, as the court already has two outstanding arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

The call for investigation comes amid a high death toll in Gaza. More than 74,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in Gaza over a span of three years, with Israeli air strikes and sniper fire continuing more than a year after an October 2025 ceasefire was agreed. The Lancet medical journal estimates the death toll is far higher once all remains are recovered, and the health ministry reported that at least 19 children were killed by Israel in Gaza alone.

cards.headline: DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi enacts law easing rules for constitutional referendum

pages.text: DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi has enacted a law that eases the rules for holding a referendum on constitutional matters. The law was enacted via an order read on national television overnight. The new legislation paves the way for changes to the constitution, a move the political opposition has condemned as an attempt by the president to cling to power. Under the current constitution, the 63-year-old Tshisekedi, who has been in power since 2019, is required to step down at the end of 2028 following the conclusion of his second five-year term.

Opposition parties have recently united to oppose efforts to change the constitution, which they argue would allow Tshisekedi to run for a third term. During a rare news conference in early May, Tshisekedi stated he had not sought a third term but added, “If people want me to have a third term, I will accept.” In response to what they termed a “constitutional coup,” the opposition organized demonstrations in the capital, Kinshasa, and other cities during June and September. The opposition, which recently formed a platform called C64, has struggled to rally large numbers of people following a landslide victory by Tshisekedi in the 2023 election. This political tension occurs while much of eastern DR Congo remains affected by conflict, including territory seized by the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group.

cards.headline: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years to protest housing costs

pages.text: Millions of people across Spain participated in a 24-hour general strike, the first of its kind in 14 years, to protest soaring housing prices. The nationwide stoppage, which was singularly called for by tenants’ associations and later backed by workers’ unions, occurred weeks before a parliamentary election on 29 November in which the far right could gain power. The Confederation of Tenants’ Association stated that approximately 4 million people had taken part by midday, representing around one-fifth of the total workforce according to other reports. While unions described the participation as massive or very significant, they noted that turnout was uneven across the country, with the strongest support reported in coastal regions such as Catalonia and Andalucía where housing costs have been particularly acute.

The strike caused widespread disruption to transport and public services. In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks, including the AP-7 motorway, which was blocked in both directions, and public transport came to a near-standstill. In Madrid, the labor action joined a continuing teachers’ strike that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions. Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or operating at minimal capacity. Sector-specific participation included 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection. Pickets were established at midnight, blocking entry to factories, markets, and transport hubs.

Clashes erupted in the evening in parts of Barcelona and Madrid. In Barcelona, groups of masked men set fire to rubbish bins and furniture, smashed shop windows, and looted stores including a Lego store. Protesters also reportedly fired fireworks toward police and attempted to enter an Apple Store. Police responded with tear gas, and the interior ministry reported dozens of arrests for various incidents. In Madrid, approximately 120,000 people joined a demonstration, while more than 50,000 people turned out in Barcelona. Amidst the disturbances, some attendees described the atmosphere as mostly peaceful and joyful, noting the presence of children and elderly people, while others reported intense fires in the streets.

cards.headline: Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu launches re-election manifesto amid economic hardship

pages.text: Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched a re-election manifesto titled *From Reform to Prosperity*, aiming to address economic growth, insecurity, and housing shortages. The manifesto, released on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), builds upon economic reforms implemented during his first term. These reforms included the removal of fuel subsidies, tax reforms, and the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates in Africa's largest oil producer. The plan sets targets for 6% annual economic growth by 2031, the addition of 78,000 security personnel, and the construction of 200,000 affordable homes. Nigeria is scheduled to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar identified as main challengers to Tinubu.

The economic reforms undertaken by Tinubu since his election in 2023 have led to significant increases in the cost of living. Joshua Osiyemi, head of Tracka—a platform launched by the non-profit BudgIT Foundation to make government financial data easier to understand—told the BBC that fuel prices rose and the cost of consumer goods skyrocketed. Osiyemi noted that a survey conducted by his organisation found most Nigerian families say they cannot survive on 10,000 naira ($7.40; £5.50) a day. Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including bread, beans, and garri (cassava flour), also saw substantial price increases.

cards.headline: Iran warns military bases in Europe could be targeted in renewed US war

pages.text: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on November 11, 2026, that Tehran could strike military bases involved in any renewed US offensive against Iran, including installations in Europe. Rezaei, a senior security figure and former commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), stated on the social media platform X that every military base involved in such aggression would be a legitimate target, extending the warning from West Asia to Europe. He emphasized that there would be “no safe distance. No safe haven. No immunity.”

The warning follows previous remarks by Kioumars Heydari, deputy chief of the Iranian Armed Forces’ General Staff, who told the Iranian broadcaster IRIB that Tehran was prepared to strike beyond the region if attacked again. Heydari stated that US bases and interests are within the range of Iranian missiles and drones, adding that countries allowing aircraft to attack Iran from their territory could face retaliatory strikes. In a separate interview with the Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen on November 11, 2026, Rezaei specifically warned that European installations could be targeted if US aircraft used them to launch attacks against Iran.

Tensions between Tehran and Washington have persisted since a US and Israeli offensive against Iran began in February. While Iran has not published an authenticated operational target list, the Iranian newspaper Kayhan has previously identified several American and NATO-linked installations that could be exposed in a wider conflict. Efforts to end the war have been complicated by disputes over sanctions, the US naval blockade, and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz. Additionally, Iran and the US remain at odds over the implementation of a June 18 memorandum of understanding reached in Islamabad.

cards.headline: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid reports of increased Russian recruitment

pages.text: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war following a reported spike in recruitment by Russia from the Southeast Asian nation. According to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project, a 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to participate in a Russian assault. The man managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after his group came under a drone attack, at which point he was captured by Ukrainian forces. The I Want to Live project reported that approximately 283 Indonesians were recruited to fight for Russia against Ukraine in the first nine months of the year, compared to no more than 10 recruited from Indonesia in the previous three years.

The Indonesian government has urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians are drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military. Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang stated that the government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure no Indonesians are recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues. Mewengkang added that Indonesia is particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking. Following these reports, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate that used social media and messaging apps to recruit its nationals.

The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions regarding the alleged recruitment effort. This follows reports of a growing number of people from African countries, including Kenya, Uganda, and South Africa, being lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022. In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

cards.headline: At least six killed in Israeli airstrike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza

pages.text: An Israeli airstrike hit a building at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, killing at least six people and wounding more than 20 others, according to the Hamas-run civil defence agency. The strike hit the surgery department of the medical complex, causing extensive damage to the intensive care and surgical wards, according to hospital officials and spokesperson Mahmoud Basal. One of the deceased is reported to be a surgeon. While Israeli Army Radio claimed the strike was an assassination operation, the hospital's director indicated the casualties were staff and patients, including individuals scheduled for surgery the following day. The Gaza civil defence, a rescue agency operating under the Hamas-run interior ministry, carried out recovery work with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The BBC is prevented by Israel from reporting independently from inside the Gaza Strip and is unable to verify the details of the incident. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told AFP they were checking for information regarding the strike.

The strike occurred amid ongoing tensions following a ceasefire agreement that took effect in October 2025. Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire, which followed two years of war triggered by an attack on Israel by the Palestinian Islamist movement on October 7, 2023. Since the start of the ceasefire, the Gaza Ministry of Health—whose figures are considered reliable by the UN—reports that more than 1,590 Palestinians have been killed. During that same period, the Israeli military has reported the loss of seven soldiers and one civilian contractor. Nasser Hospital, the largest medical facility in southern Gaza, was previously hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025 that killed at least 20 people, including health workers and journalists. On November 10, 2026, local emergency services reported that Israeli forces killed seven people, including a 13-year-old boy, in the Gaza Strip; the Israeli military stated it had targeted military operatives.

cards.headline: Brazil's top electoral court fines Meta $1.34 million for failing to comply with judicial orders

pages.text: Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on November 10, 2026, to impose a 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) fine on Meta, the US tech giant that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. The court determined that Meta failed to fully comply with judicial orders during the presidential election by missing deadlines and lacking transparency in its investigation. While the fine was issued, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome. Reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that no preliminary evidence indicated intentional actions were taken to influence the election, noting that such a conclusion would require robust evidence produced through appropriate legal proceedings.

The ruling follows a complaint filed by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition ahead of the October 25 runoff vote. The coalition accused Meta of using algorithmic manipulation to favor his far-right rival, Flavio Bolsonaro. Meta told the court it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns and stated it will defend itself against what it called 'false allegations.'

cards.headline: Trump defends war against Iran during Veterans Day address

pages.text: President Donald Trump defended the war against Iran during a U.S. Veterans Day commemoration at Arlington National Cemetery near Washington. Speaking to troops, veterans, and administration officials, Trump stated that the conflict would soon end and leave the world a safer and more peaceful place. He asserted that the war was initiated by Tehran, which he said has been waging war on America since 1979, and maintained that U.S. forces are acting to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon. The war began on February 28 with strikes by the U.S. and Israel against Iran. According to the latest Pentagon figures, the conflict has resulted in the deaths of 23 U.S. service members and wounded several hundred more.

During the ceremony, Trump praised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, stating he had “done a fantastic job.” Hegseth's leadership has faced recent political challenges; on November 10, 2026, Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives blocked an impeachment effort against him. That effort, launched by an outgoing Republican lawmaker, alleged that Hegseth abused his powers as Pentagon chief and waged war without congressional authorization. Hegseth also faced a public reprimand at the cemetery when an army sentinel watching over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier called out a small group that included Hegseth, his wife, and several aides. The sentinel, who halted a patrol to demand that visitors maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect, reprimanded the group after some members laughed following a photo taken in front of the sacred site.

cards.headline: Lack of safeguards in Bangladesh Qawmi madrasas leaves children vulnerable to abuse

pages.text: Approximately 25,000 Qawmi madrasas in Bangladesh educate an estimated 70 lakh students, but many of these non-governmental Islamic schools lack enforceable child protection policies and necessary safety measures. Weak oversight and inconsistent complaint mechanisms have left children vulnerable to abuse, particularly in institutions with dormitories. Recent allegations involving more than two dozen students across several districts regarding sexual abuse, physical assault, and intimidation have highlighted these institutional failures and the lack of reliable channels for children to seek redress.

In one reported incident in Gazipur, eight-year-old Abu Sufian (not his real name) was enrolled in the residential section of a Qawmi madrasa on October 7 after his parents were persuaded by a teacher. Having previously attended the school as a day-shift student for two years, Sufian returned home four days later appearing lethargic and feverish, with bruises on his hands, throat, tongue, and buttocks. Sufian told his mother that a teacher allegedly gave him a mobile phone to watch cartoons at night before sexually assaulting him for three consecutive nights. The teacher also allegedly covered the dormitory's CCTV camera with clothes and threatened to kill the boy if he disclosed the abuse.

cards.headline: Bomb hoaxes targeting thousands of European schools cause widespread evacuations

pages.text: Thousands of schools across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats, prompting evacuations and adding to a series of disruptions across the continent. In Italy, the Education Ministry reported that 6,000 schools received emailed bomb alerts, resulting in a sizable number of schools sending students home. At 10 a.m. local time, 312 Italian schools received an identical email stating, “A powerful explosive device with a remote detonator has been left in your building.” While most affected schools were in Rome, several other major Italian cities also received the message. Similar warnings were sent to hundreds of schools in Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland, as well as in Bulgaria.

Authorities in Italy, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland stated the threats did not appear credible. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a social media statement that law enforcement and government institutions are working to monitor the situation and reassure citizens, families, and school staff, noting that investigations have found no evidence of a concrete danger. Despite the lack of evidence of a real threat, the Italian government has expressed concerns regarding possible hybrid warfare—actions intended to destabilize a target through non-traditional means such as cyberattacks or disinformation. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the hoaxes were designed to “sow terror” for thousands of families, while Antonello Giannelli, head of the National Association of School Principals, described the incident as the work of a hoaxer attempting to sow chaos.

On the afternoon of November 11, 2026, Prime Minister Meloni chaired an emergency government meeting to address the reports. The wave of school hoaxes follows other recent disruptions in Europe, including grounded flights and the hacking of supermarket refrigerators. Governments are currently attempting to determine the origins and motives behind these incidents, which some describe as part of a string of coordinated attacks aimed at destabilizing life in the continent.

cards.headline: German tech company Singulus Technologies signs €60 million contract with Elon Musk for Starmind satellite solar cells

pages.text: Singulus Technologies, a medium-sized German technology company, has signed a €60 million order with SpaceX founder Elon Musk to supply solar cells for a new line of satellites called Starmind. According to a statement from Musk on X, this major order is the first of many. The solar cells will be supplied to the SpaceX Starmind satellites manufacturing site in Texas in early 2027. Following the announcement, Singulus Technologies' stock temporarily spiked by 65% to 80%, valuing the firm at approximately €73 million. This rise follows a 2025 annual revenue of €48.3 million for the company. As part of a strategic partnership, plans are in place to create further facilities and production lines to reach a solar power production capacity of 100 gigawatts, which is the equivalent of the annual production of ten large nuclear reactors.

The Starmind project aims to create what Musk described as a 'sentient sun' by producing satellites that function as AI data centres in space. These satellites are intended to compute AI data in orbit and transmit it to Earth via laser. To power these operations, the Starmind satellite constellation will be equipped with solar wings measuring 75 meters long. In a filing at the Federal Communications Commission, Musk stated that by harnessing near-constant solar power with low operating and maintenance costs, the satellites will achieve cost and energy efficiency while reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centres. While Musk has claimed a plan to launch 1 million satellites for this project, the technology has not yet proven itself; however, Google has expressed similar plans to use satellites as computing units for AI calculations by harnessing the sun.

cards.headline: Trinidad and Tobago highest court overturns law criminalizing gay sex

pages.text: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the UK-based final court of appeal for British dependencies and overseas territories, issued a unanimous decision overturning a law in Trinidad and Tobago that criminalized gay sex. The ruling concludes a decade-long legal battle led by LGBT+ Trinidadian activists and dictates that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act cannot be used to prosecute private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex. Under the previous law, individuals faced sentences of two years for “serious indecency” and five years for “buggery.”

In its decision, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council stated that constitutional rights must be interpreted to be “practical and effective in the present day, not in the past.” Freedom Law Chambers, the firm representing activist Jason Jones, described the judgment as a “phenomenal victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago.” UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk called the ruling a significant milestone for rights and equality, expressing hope that it helps remove longstanding sources of stigma, exclusion, barriers, and violence experienced by Trinidadians and Tobagonians based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
Following the verdict, Jason Jones stated he intends to engage in targeted activism in the coming months regarding how the Caribbean, beyond just Trinidad and Tobago, deals with endemic homophobia.

cards.headline: US charges three Iran-backed suspects with plotting 18 attacks in US and Europe

pages.text: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) unsealed an indictment on November 10, 2026, charging three men with terrorism offenses for allegedly orchestrating a campaign of approximately 18 attacks and attempted attacks across the United States and Europe. Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah, both of which are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations. The suspects allegedly operated under the name Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which prosecutors claim was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah. The targets of these plots included Jewish communities and a British air base hosting American troops. The three charged individuals are Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian; Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi national; and Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, 32, a dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen.

The indictment alleges the suspects directed several attacks remotely using FaceTime. In April, prosecutors claim the three men watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via the video calling app, with al-Hassani allegedly coaching an attacker on how to ignite and hurl incendiary devices while al-Saadi filmed. The following day, al-Hassani allegedly guided another man via video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London, reportedly telling the attacker to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The campaign included arson, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London, one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen. While the indictment does not specify the locations of all plots, it notes that the United Kingdom was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, with as many as seven of the attacks taking place there.

One major incident occurred on 27 September near RAF Fairford in the United Kingdom, a base where US armed forces were stationed. A major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base, leading the US to remove all its bombers from the site. The DOJ alleges al-Hassani orchestrated this terrorist plot at the air force base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK in connection with the RAF Fairford incident. According to the indictment, al-Hassani and Mohajeri were both in Iran at the time of the September incident. Meanwhile, al-Saadi was allegedly coordinating with the pair through third parties from a New York prison, where he has been awaiting trial on previous charges since his arrest in August. Al-Saadi is scheduled for a court appearance on 19 November, though it is unclear if this routine status conference relates to the new terrorism charges or his previous case.

cards.headline: Bangladesh introduces lottery and written exams for private school admissions

pages.text: The Ministry of Education in Bangladesh has introduced a new admission policy for private educational institutions that uses a lottery system for class 1 and written exams for classes 2 to 9. Issued by the Secondary and Higher Education Division on November 10, 2026, the Student Admission Policy-2027 aims to increase transparency and discipline in the admission process across the country. Under the new rules, students seeking entry into class 1 will be selected via lottery, while admission for classes 2 through 9 will be determined by written exams in Mathematics, English, and Bangla to fill vacant seats. For class 1 applicants, children must be older than six years but younger than seven years as of January 1, 2027, though students with special needs are eligible for an age relaxation of up to five years.

cards.headline: Around 230 families left homeless following house demolitions in Dhalpur City Polli, Bangladesh

pages.text: Around 230 families have been left homeless after their houses were demolished at Dhalpur City Polli in Bangladesh. Residents alleged that the eviction occurred despite a High Court ruling that directed authorities not to evict them until proper rehabilitation arrangements were made. Many of the affected families, described as mostly economically disadvantaged, stated they had lived in the settlement for decades. cards.headline: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food insecurity, UN warns

pages.text: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food insecurity, according to a warning from the United Nations. A joint statement by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and the Lebanese agriculture ministry reported that nearly a quarter of the population faces crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse. The UN bodies called for “urgent action” to address the situation, noting that the number of people affected is expected to rise to 1.15 million by the middle of the year. The UN defines these levels of food insecurity as households facing malnutrition or being only able to meet minimum needs through emergency measures, such as selling assets.

The food crisis follows years of war and an unprecedented economic collapse that began in 2019. The UN stated that employment opportunities remain limited, savings have been depleted, and debt remains high, while the rising cost of food, fuel, and other essentials continues to strain household budgets. The UN expressed particular concern regarding conditions in conflict-affected areas of south Lebanon, as well as in impoverished regions in the north and east of the country.

Lebanon has endured two successive wars with neighboring Israel since 2023. Lebanese authorities estimate the cost of the two wars between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah since October 2023 is approximately $27 billion. The last war, launched in March in support of Hezbollah’s patron Iran, displaced more than one million people in Lebanon; that number fell to around 300,000 after violence subsided in June.

cards.headline: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo exceeds 11,000 cases

pages.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed 11,000 cases, according to Congolese government data. The Bundibugyo virus, which has no known vaccine or treatment, has infected 11,042 people and killed 5,387, according to the health ministry. This represents nearly half of those infected and marks the country's deadliest outbreak. The virus has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces and has also reached Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria. While the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that almost 3,000 people have recovered and transmission is slowing in some areas, the outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern. The current situation has already resulted in at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared in mid-May compared to the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak, which saw 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

Authorities are struggling to contain the disease due to armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads, and rainy weather. Insecurity has become a major obstacle to the response. During an attack on the town of Cantine-Aloya, 66 civilians were killed, including three health workers, and three health facilities were looted and burned. In Tshopo province, a nurse was killed and another health worker was badly injured during an attack while responding to an Ebola alert. Other incidents include a grenade found near a health zone office and stones thrown at a vehicle conducting safe and dignified burials. These attacks, along with violence fueled by mistrust and misinformation, have targeted medical professionals and facilities. Health authorities are calling for a halt to fighting in the Ituri and North Kivu provinces to allow unhindered access to the sick. Additionally, more than 1,000 contacts have been lost to follow up, and three confirmed cases are unaccounted for.

cards.headline: Former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani found dead in Beirut apartment

Lebanese security and judicial investigators are looking into whether Al-Alwani was deliberately lured to the city and if political motives were behind the killing. Preliminary findings from a Lebanese judicial source indicate the 57-year-old was strangled and had been struck on the head. Al-Alwani’s office described the death as a “premeditated assassination” and a “treacherous crime,” calling for a transparent investigation to identify those who planned and carried out the act. Lebanon’s top prosecutor, Judge Ahmed Rami al-Hajj, is personally overseeing the investigation, which is being conducted by the Information Branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.

Investigators are focusing on individuals who reportedly met Al-Alwani at Beirut’s Rafic Hariri International Airport following his arrival on November 5 and accompanied him to an apartment in the Afif Al-Tibi area of Tariq Al-Jadideh. A Lebanese national suspected of involvement has been arrested, and authorities are searching for two Syrian suspects who remain at large. A judicial source told Arab News that investigators are not ruling out the possibility that the perpetrators were Iraqi nationals rather than Syrian. While initial, unconfirmed reports suggested three individuals were suspected of involvement, subsequent information indicated two people were under suspicion, while a third was believed to have been a taxi driver. Lebanese security agencies are reviewing surveillance footage and questioning individuals who were in contact with Al-Alwani to track his movements from his arrival until his body was discovered.

The body was discovered after a real estate agent, attempting to contact Al-Alwani to request an additional payment and extend a two-day, $200 rental agreement, noticed a foul odor coming from the 12th-floor apartment. The agent found the body inside the bathroom, and it was initially transferred to a hospital morgue. cards.headline: US House Republicans block impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

pages.text: On November 10, 2026, the US House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 to refer impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee. The vote effectively blocked an impeachment bid introduced by Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who had warned that referring the resolution to a committee would kill the initiative because of the limited time remaining in the current Congress. Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, was the only Republican to oppose the procedural move to refer the matter to the committee. Following the vote, Massie compared his Republican colleagues in the outgoing Congress to passengers on the Titanic, stating, “They know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board.”

The impeachment resolution brought eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. Massie accused the Defense Secretary of waging war on Iran without congressional authorization and of abuse of power. The articles also included allegations regarding strikes against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie described as “extrajudicial killings,” as well as the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Additionally, Massie accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech after an attempt to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video in which Kelly urged military and intelligence personnel to stand up against illegal orders. During a Pentagon press conference on November 10, 2026, Hegseth dismissed the accusations as “slander,” “sabotage,” a “farce,” and a “stunt.”

President Trump celebrated the outcome on Truth Social, stating the effort “has miserably FAILED” and describing Hegseth as a “Great American Patriot” who had been “exonerated.” Vice President JD Vance also commented that Hegseth had “obviously not” committed impeachable offenses. cards.headline: Millions participate in Spain's first general strike in 14 years to protest rising housing costs

pages.text: Millions of people across Spain joined a nationwide 24-hour general strike to protest a deepening housing crisis. The stoppage, which was called for by tenants' associations and later backed by workers' unions, saw approximately four million people take part by midday, according to the Confederation of Tenants’ Association. This marks the first general strike in the country in 14 years and occurs weeks before a snap election scheduled for November 29, in which the far right could potentially gain power. The housing crisis has become a central political debate, following the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid. According to estimates from the central bank, Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, a figure set to grow to more than a million by 2028. As fewer families can afford to buy, the number of renters has risen sharply; Spain's youth council reports the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315), which is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.

Participation in the strike was reported as high across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, though unions noted participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions such as Catalonia and Andalusia, where housing costs have been particularly acute. In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks, some using burning tyres, as public transport came to a near-standstill and key roads, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked in both directions. In Madrid, thousands of demonstrators entered the city's main boulevard, temporarily halting traffic, and scuffles occurred between picketers and police near the country's main wholesale market. Strikers at the Mercamadrid wholesale market reported that police used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention. Additionally, some airlines reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain due to participation by airport and airline workers.

The strike follows political friction regarding housing legislation. The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass laws to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. While Sanchez's government approved two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the rejected housing reforms, Sanchez called the early November 29 election in hopes of shoring up support. The government stated the strike is being held “in favor of rights” rather than against anyone, though sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have suggested it is “against the opposition.” In Madrid, the labor action added to an ongoing strike by teachers that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions. The general strike also follows a strike by rail workers the previous day regarding two major deadly train crashes.

cards.headline: Two U.S. companies apply for deep-sea mining exploration licenses in South Pacific international waters

pages.text: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. The applications seek to explore the seabed for mining potential with the eventual goal of extracting and selling minerals. The targeted areas include a 101,064-square-kilometer (39,021-square-mile) pocket of international waters bounded by the exclusive economic zones of the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia, as well as an 89,645-km2 (34,612-mi2) area south of the Cook Islands’ exclusive economic zone. The applicants are Delaware-incorporated American Deep Sea Minerals, Inc. (ADSM) and Florida-based American Ocean Minerals Corporation (AOM).

The applications are part of a broader effort by U.S. companies to stake claims to the international seabed through a U.S. permitting process. This process bypasses the U.N.-linked multilateral body responsible for regulating deep-sea mining on the high seas and protecting the marine environment. Beyond the South Pacific sites, a Mongabay investigation showed that U.S. companies are also seeking rights through this process for large seabed blocks in international waters near Guam in the western Pacific and in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), a vast area located between Hawai‘i and Mexico. These areas often contain polymetallic nodules, which are avocado-sized rocks containing minerals such as nickel, manganese, copper, and cobalt.

Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back against the applications. Louisa Castledine, a spokesperson for the Cook Islands-based ocean advocacy collective Ocean Ancestors, told Mongabay that the plans create a “dangerous pathway of opening up the Pacific region to increased exploitation and vulnerability.” Castledine stated that the companies are testing “every kind of trajectory and angle and strategy and opportunity they can make to extract.”

cards.headline: EU weighs upgrading ties with Syria to counter Russian influence

pages.text: The European Union is considering a broad upgrade in its relationship with Syria, including security sector reform, investment, and the revival of a long-frozen trade accord. According to an EU document seen by Reuters, the bloc aims to draw Damascus closer to Europe and counter the lingering influence of Russia following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad. The discussion paper was prepared by the EU's diplomatic service ahead of a November 16 meeting of EU foreign ministers. It represents one of the bloc's most ambitious efforts to normalize ties with Syria less than two years after the fall of the Assad regime ended decades of authoritarian rule.

The EU's diplomatic service noted that while Syria's transition is moving forward, challenges remain high. The bloc stated that accelerated progress is needed regarding economic recovery, national reconciliation, and the reintegration of refugees and internally displaced people. To support security-sector reform, the EU is considering trilateral cooperation with Jordan to train Syrian police recruits. These efforts are intended to limit the influence of Russia and other foreign actors in Syria, according to the discussion paper. While the document noted that Moscow's influence has diminished since the post-Assad transition, its continued economic leverage and military presence remain a concern.

Russia previously intervened in Syria's civil war to support the Assad government and secure strategic Mediterranean assets, including the Hmeimim air base and the Tartous naval facility. Since the overthrow, the Kremlin has attempted to secure a new deal with current Syrian authorities to maintain access to these sites. To deepen ties, the EU is proposing to revive an association agreement that was initialled in 2008 but never concluded. This agreement would provide a framework for political dialogue, free trade, and broader cooperation. EU diplomats intend to seek a fresh mandate from EU member countries to negotiate revisions to the pact, using the existing text as a basis for deepening relations.

cards.headline: Canada Post issues stamp honoring Chinese Canadians who performed covert World War II operations

pages.text: Canada Post has issued a new Remembrance Day stamp to honor approximately 150 Chinese Canadians who volunteered for dangerous covert operations during World War II. Although these individuals were barred from serving in the Canadian military at the start of the war, they volunteered for secret missions in 1944 when called upon. The stamp was unveiled in Vancouver on Nov. 3, and a ceremony was held in Toronto on Nov. 10, 2026, alongside the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto. The design features a historic black-and-white photograph of Force 136 members awaiting repatriation in 1945, overlaid with the red phoenix insignia of Force 136, with the group's name appearing in English, French, and traditional Chinese.

The honored group consisted of Chinese Canadians recruited for their language skills and their ability to blend in while conducting secret missions behind enemy lines in Japanese-occupied Asia. These volunteers served either with Force 136—a unit of Britain’s Special Operations Executive—or with Australia’s Services Reconnaissance Department. To prepare for these roles, they underwent specialized training in espionage, sabotage, guerrilla warfare, parachuting, and intelligence gathering. Historians noted that the service of Force 136 members helped advance the Allied war effort and contributed to the push for equality within Canada.

At the time of their service, Chinese Canadians faced discrimination and were considered second-class citizens denied basic rights. Many volunteers viewed enlistment as a way to demonstrate commitment to Canada and influence how immigrants were treated. Following the war, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed two years later, allowing Chinese Canadians to gain full citizenship rights, including the right to vote. Sharifa Khan of the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto stated that the recognition by Canada Post is important for telling these stories to future generations of all Canadians.

cards.headline: 237-million-year-old fossils in China reveal armored sea-dwelling amphibian

pages.text: Two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons discovered in China's Guizhou Province reveal an ancient amphibian, *Gerrothorax maritimus*, that lived entirely in the ocean. This finding is notable because no amphibian known to be alive on November 11, 2026, is known to live its entire life in a marine environment. While mammals, reptiles, and birds include species that live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water, scientists had not previously identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with this ability. Among more than 8,000 amphibian species living on November 11, 2026, fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt, and none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments. The fossils date back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period, a time when the Guizhou region was submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses. The unusual animal had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was approximately the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe *Gerrothorax maritimus* spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery was made by an international team of researchers from the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings were published in *Nature Ecology & Evolution*. Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis and the study's corresponding author, stated that the team has been studying the ecosystem of this area to reconstruct it. cards.headline: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests amino acids may have originated in different parts of the solar system

pages.text: Analysis of amino acids from the Bennu asteroid and the Murchison meteorite suggests that these molecules, which are the building blocks of proteins necessary for life, may have formed through the same process but originated in different locations within the solar system. Researchers found that the carbon and nitrogen atoms within these molecules likely came from different reservoirs, according to a study published in Communications Earth & Environment. This finding provides a potential link between space chemistry and the origins of life on Earth by tracing the history of the atoms that compose these essential organic compounds.

To reach these conclusions, a research team including scientists from Penn State used a technique to study isotopes, which are slight variations in the mass of an atom within a molecular compound. Because isotope ratios act as a measurable tag, they can link specific molecules to the chemical processes or reservoirs where they were formed. By measuring these isotopes, the team could identify clues regarding the older history of specific atoms within the amino acids. The study utilized unique isotope instruments, including one located only at Penn State, to examine samples from the Bennu asteroid—delivered in 2023 by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission—and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969.

The researchers reported that the wide range of isotope values measured in both the Bennu and Murchison samples was surprising. This variation suggests that the carbon and nitrogen atoms within the amino acids did not originate from a single source. Lead author Ophélie Mcintosh, a former postdoctoral researcher in Penn State's Department of Geosciences, noted that while most studies focus on the quantity and distribution of amino acids, their research focused on how they are formed. The Bennu sample provided specific insight because it was delivered directly from space without terrestrial contamination.

cards.headline: Gravitational waves could reveal new exoplanets, according to NASA-led studies

pages.text: Two studies led by NASA astrophysicists suggest the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) observatory could detect a unique population of exoplanets—worlds outside our solar system—by observing gravitational waves. These waves are tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, detail how LISA could identify planets orbiting double white dwarf systems, which are binary pairs of white dwarfs in tight orbits. While the possibility of detecting exoplanets around these systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008, these new studies provide more detail on the detection method and potential confirmation processes.

The first study, authored by Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, examines the detection method. McGrath determined the specific planet masses and orbital periods where this method would work most effectively. The detection process is similar to radial velocity, a method that uses light to find exoplanets around nearby stars. In the case of LISA, an exoplanet's presence would become imprinted on the gravitational wave signal produced by the orbiting white dwarfs. A second paper, by McGrath and co-authors, investigates how these planets could be confirmed using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.

LISA is a mission led by the European Space Agency (ESA) that is currently in development and slated for launch in the mid-2030s. NASA is a collaborative partner in the mission, contributing telescopes, critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support. The observatory is designed to detect gravitational waves to help scientists better understand the universe.

cards.headline: Cambodia’s mangrove forests provide refuge for threatened wildlife, study finds

pages.text: A seven-year study conducted by the Phnom Penh-based private company Fishing Cat Ecological Enterprise (FCEE) found that Cambodia’s mangrove forests and associated wetlands serve as critical refuge for several threatened and elusive species. Researchers deployed camera traps across 156 coastal and riverine mangrove sites within the Peam Krasop Wildlife Sanctuary and the adjacent Koh Kapik Ramsar site between 2017 and 2023. These two areas together form Cambodia’s largest mangrove expanse. While the research team initially focused on the fishing cat, they expanded their scope to include other mammal species to support broader conservation efforts, according to FCEE director and study corresponding author Vanessa Herranz Muñoz.

Camera footage from the study identified several threatened species utilizing the habitat. These included fishing cats (Prionailurus viverrinus) in mangrove thickets, smooth-coated otters (Lutra perspicillata) in fringe river channels, leopard cats (Prionailurus bengalensis) and hairy-nosed otters (Lutra sumatrana) near rivers, and large-spotted civets (Viverra megaspila) in swamp forests dominated by paperbark trees (Melaleuca spp.). Despite the presence of these animals, researchers observed that four threatened species declined over the seven-year study period: the endangered long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), the endangered large-spotted civet, and the vulnerable fishing cat and smooth-coated otter. The adaptable common palm civet (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus) was the only species to show signs of increase. The critically endangered Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) and the endangered hairy-nosed otter remained difficult to detect.

Vanessa Herranz Muñoz noted that conservation efforts must extend beyond mangrove forests to include surrounding ecosystems. She stated that protecting Melaleuca forests is essential for the endangered large-spotted civet, while riverine mixed mangroves are critical for the hairy-nosed otter, which is considered the rarest otter in the world. A 2023 biodiversity survey conducted by the conservation NGO Fauna & Flora and the FCEE, which also involved Herranz Muñoz, identified more than 700 unique species within the Peam Krasop and Koh Kapik areas.

cards.headline: Coyote populations persist on North Carolina's Outer Banks despite removal efforts

pages.text: Coyote populations on the Outer Banks of North Carolina appear to be a permanent fixture, persisting despite long-term lethal removal programs intended to protect shore-nesting birds and sea turtles. A study by North Carolina State University researchers found that between 45 and 60 coyotes inhabit the islands at any one time, even as the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service work to manage their impact on local wildlife nesting habitats. Over the course of the study, researchers identified 62 individual coyotes through DNA analysis of fecal samples collected across seven islands: Bodie, Pea, Hatteras, Ocracoke, North Core, South Core, and Shackleford Banks. This research represents the first peer-reviewed study to estimate coyote density and population size on any barrier island.

The study, conducted over three seasons between 2024 and 2025, suggests that removal efforts face significant challenges due to population turnover. In 2024, the National Park Service removed 14 coyotes from Bodie and Hatteras islands, yet researchers continued to detect coyotes on both islands throughout the year as new individuals replaced those that were removed. Lead author Daniel Sossover, a research associate in the Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources at NC State University and at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences, noted that the National Park Service has spent significant funds for more than a decade attempting to manage the coyotes through lethal removal. Sossover stated that the findings suggest a need to recognize coyotes as part of the ecosystem and find ways to coexist with them. The study's collaborators included NC State University professors Roland Kays and Liz Kierepka, and Nathan Hostetter of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Coyotes have moved into the Outer Banks over the last two decades, likely by swimming between islands or crossing bridges. This expansion has caused ecological and management concerns for residents, visitors, and wildlife managers. From 2009 to 2025, the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lethally removed more than 170 coyotes from Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Cape Lookout National Seashore, and Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge. Sossover indicated that removal often fails because coyote populations may respond to heavy removal pressure by breeding earlier, producing larger litter sizes, or moving into removal areas, allowing local populations to bounce back rapidly.

cards.headline: Researchers identify geological sources of blue azurite used by Ancestral Pueblo communities

pages.text: A research team led by Kari Schleher of the University of New Mexico has identified the geological sources of azurite used by Ancestral Pueblo communities approximately 1,400 years ago. Azurite is a copper mineral with a vivid blue color that was used as a pigment or paint. The study, according to a statement from the University of New Mexico, focused on 12 azurite specimens recovered in the Four Corners region of the American Southwest. By analyzing the isotopes of lead, strontium, and copper in these specimens, scientists were able to trace the material back to specific locations. Most of the analyzed samples were found to have been collected in the Lisbon Valley, while two samples originated from the Zuni Mountains in New Mexico.

To determine the origins of the pigment, the scientists first analyzed two samples of azurite from known mining sites in New Mexico and Utah used by Ancestral Pueblo people. This provided a baseline for comparing the 12 specimens found in the Four Corners region. Future research by the team will include analyzing more azurite samples held at the New Mexico Mining Museum. Schleher also stated that the team plans to consult local oral histories regarding traditional territories and the use of mines.
